title: Temporomandibular dysfunction (TMD) in patients with SAPHO syndrome
summary:
Patients with rare diseases often wait an average of 4–5 years before receiving a diagnosis. Among the approximately 8,000 known rare diseases is SAPHO syndrome. About 15% of rare diseases affect the oral, jaw, and facial region. Because dentists usually see their patients at least once a year for routine check-ups, they could play an important role in recognizing early signs of rare diseases. However, studies have shown that most dentists have only limited knowledge of rare diseases. This is also reflected in the research on SAPHO syndrome: Although there are case reports describing involvement of the temporomandibular joint, there are no studies specifically addressing temporomandibular joint problems in patients with SAPHO syndrome.
This study aims to examine patients with SAPHO syndrome and a control group for TMD symptoms and signs. The examination will be based on a standardized questionnaire and a clinical examination.

interventions.name:
Arm 1: SAPHO Group
Assessment of patients with a confirmed diagnosis of SAPHO syndrome. The diagnostic process follows the DC/TMD criteria and includes standardized questionnaires as well as a clinical functional examination.

Arm 2: Control Group
Age- and sex-matched control participants, randomly recruited. They undergo the same DC/TMD-based diagnostic procedures as the SAPHO group.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients who have been diagnosed with SAPHO syndrome by experts in rare diseases
Exclusion criteria:
-Psychological impairments that prevent understanding of the questionnaire, the study, or the ability to provide informed consent
-Refusal to participate in the study
-Lack of capacity to provide informed consent
-Patients with Total Temporomandibular Joint Replacement (TMJ)
-Patients under the age of 18
